docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: Productions
docs.text:
One production. Two dates, ever — everything else about a show is a join.

Grain

One opening night - is what we'll say for now. Productions may share the same NAME and will generally serve the same then (maybe the'ats what we build?)

docs.title: 🔴 TWO DATES, EVER
docs.text:
date_FirstRehearsal + date_Opening. Both are contractual facts about the show — negotiated with a director, true whether or not anyone ever prints a calendar. Both are typed by hand and can never be derived.

The hard line: a third production-level date is an EVENT, not a field. Designer deadline, build start, photo call — those move, repeat, or are one of many. Events already have a table, an import pipe, and a canonical type layer.

A date that can move, repeat, or be one of many is an EVENT. A date that is a defining property of the entity is a field.

docs.title: What is NOT here
docs.text:
• 🔴 The page bounds live on [PRODUCTION_CALENDARS] — "needed first/last" are page dimensions wearing dates (nothing happens on "last date needed"; legacy fed it straight into CalendarDaysNeeded). Proof: the same show in two time blocks needs different page bounds and the SAME first rehearsal.
  • Director is an [ASSIGNMENTS] row, not a field. So are course codes.
  • 🚫 No convenience copy of anything. A calendar reads first rehearsal through fkProduction — that is what the relationship is for. A lookup that copies the value goes stale silently the first time a director moves the start date.

docs.title: The placement rule (generalizes to every field)
docs.text:
A date belongs to the table whose GRAIN it is one-per-of. One first rehearsal per production. One needed-first/last per calendar. Settles the next forty fields without another conversation.

⚠️ The legacy file could not make this distinction: it had no PRODUCTIONS table, every date was a global on a one-record singleton, so "which entity owns this" was unanswerable. The duplication was inherited confusion, not a design choice.

Never mutate. remove notes Strips <...> the same way Same CREATE_multipleDays A multi-day event is DUPLICATED into one record per day, flagged autoGenerated=1 🔴 Needs a decision — EVENTS grain is currently one row per event. • import Records — Show All → Delete All Records → Import. REPLACE THE SET deletes again before calling it. Double delete, and the reason history is impossible → UPSERT on TaskID + fkProduction.

docs.title: ADAPTER_ClickUp_Pull
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: ADAPTER_ClickUp_Pull
docs.text:
The only script that knows ClickUp's task-page shape. Pages a view, caches each task in xt_RECORDS, and writes a pull event for every new or changed task.

Grain

One page of tasks per iteration. One xt_RECORDS row and one sync_EVENTS row per new or changed task.

docs.title: The endpoint
docs.text:
GET {baseURL}/view/{viewPath}/task?page={n}, returning { "tasks" : [ ... ], "last_page" : true|false }. Each task carries id, name, status, date_updated and custom_fields.

Authorization is the personal token, bare (no Bearer prefix), matching the convention ADAPTER_ClickUp_RefreshFields already uses.

docs.title: What happens per task
docs.text:
For each task on the page, the script looks up its xt_RECORDS row by xt_ID and fk_xtContainer:

  • No row: creates the xt_RECORDS row (container, id, label, version), then writes a pull event with the full task JSON as the response. This is a new record, and the dispatcher will adopt it.
  • Row exists, same version: the task has not changed since the last pull. No event, no update.
  • Row exists, different version: updates xt_Label and xt_Version on the existing row, then writes a pull event. The dispatcher will run the three-way compare against this record's newest prior event.

An event is only written for a new or changed task. Unchanged tasks are never logged. This follows D-048 ruling 1: an event only for a new or changed task.

docs.title: The version check
docs.text: xt_Version stores ClickUp's date_updated as raw milliseconds text. The comparison is Exact, so there is no type coercion. Equal means unchanged, and the pull moves on. This is the cheapest possible skip, and it is the reason the pull can be run frequently without drowning sync_EVENTS in identical payloads.

docs.title: Development cap
docs.text: A variable $devCap at the top of the script controls whether the pull stops after page 0. Set to 1 (the default), it caps the pull at 30 tasks, which is checkpoint 2 of the sync plan. Set to 0 for a full pull once the adoption and compare paths are proven.

docs.title: Page-level errors
docs.text: A page-level error (transport failure, non-200, double-429) is not a sync event. The script exits with an error JSON, and SYNC_Run reports it. The session row exists: its absence of events tells you it failed before any task was processed. This ruling follows from the principle that every sync_EVENTS row has a record key.

docs.title: 429 handling
docs.text: A 429 pauses 60 seconds and retries the page once. A second failure exits with the error. The sync plan places retry logic here, in the pull, where it is worth the complexity, and not in the housekeeping refresh scripts.

docs.title: Event field names
docs.text: Uses fk_vAction (the VALUES PrimaryKey for PULL) with stored_ActionLabel snapped to "PULL", matching the value-list keying convention from D-051. The PULL key is looked up once at the top of the script by ExecuteSQL against value_LISTS and VALUES, so a renamed value breaks the lookup rather than silently writing the wrong key.

docs.title: D-043 gap
docs.text: Field names in all ExecuteSQL calls are literal text, same gap as SYNC_Run and the refresh scripts. The sql/ custom-function family is not built.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
The xt_RECORDS lookup per task is an ExecuteSQL call inside a loop. At 30 tasks per page that is 30 calls, each indexed. At the volumes this file handles, that is nothing. If the page size ever increases to hundreds, batch the IDs and search once.

The full task JSON is stored in sync_EVENTS::Response for every new or changed task. That is the correct design (it is the base for the three-way compare), but it means sync_EVENTS can grow large. It is the one table that cannot be published from a public repo without FERPA clearance.

docs.title: ADAPTER_ClickUp_RefreshFields
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: ADAPTER_ClickUp_RefreshFields
docs.text:
The first script in the file that calls ClickUp. Fills xt_FIELDS names and types from the list's custom-field endpoint, and reports a mapped field ClickUp no longer has.

Grain

One container per run. Writes xt_FieldName and xt_FieldType on its xt_FIELDS rows and nothing else.

docs.title: The endpoint
docs.text:
GET {BaseURL}/list/{list id}/field, returning { "fields" : [ { id, name, type, type_config } ] }. Verified against the Claris-independent ClickUp custom fields reference on 2026-10-23.

The personal token goes in Authorization bare. No Bearer prefix: that form is for OAuth access tokens, and a personal token sent as a bearer is rejected. Tokens begin pk_.

docs.title: What it writes, and what it refuses to
docs.text:
It writes the name and the type. It never writes mapKey, and that restraint is the point: mapKey is the only thing that survives ClickUp renaming a field, and it is the reason the list's two identically named Phone Number fields cannot be confused. A refresh that corrected mapKey from ClickUp would hand the naming collision straight back.

It also never writes xt_FieldID. The id is the contract.

docs.title: Four counts, because three of them are defects
docs.text:
The closing dialog reports:

  • Updated — rows that matched a live ClickUp field.
  • Native, skipped — rows with an empty xt_FieldID, meaning name and status. Task attributes, not custom fields, so there is nothing to refresh and this is expected to read 2.
  • Mapped but missing from ClickUp — a row whose id ClickUp did not return. The field was deleted, or moved out of this list. This is the one to act on: the mapping is now pointing at nothing, and without this count a pull would simply read empty for that field forever and nobody would know why.
  • On the list but not mapped — fields ClickUp has that xt_FIELDS does not. Informational, and expected to be large, since the list carries availability, positions, relationships and more that this sync deliberately ignores.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: Reads BaseURL and Token off the xt_SYSTEMS row itself, from the key the dispatcher passed. Nothing sensitive travels in a script parameter, where it would be visible in the Data Viewer and in any dialog that echoes the parameter.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
The inner loop rescans the JSON array per row, so the cost is rows × fields. At ten rows against a list of this size that is nothing, and the flat shape is worth more than the speed. If a container ever maps dozens of fields, build a lookup once instead.

The HTTP status is read from the first line of the dumped header with MiddleWords, paired with Get ( LastError ) so a transport failure and a non-200 are both caught. A 429 is not retried here: that belongs in the pull, where it is worth the complexity, not in a housekeeping script run by hand.

docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: refresh | Target_Tables
docs.text:
The app catalog refresh as installed in URITP People. Body lives on the standards shelf; this page carries the install values and the first run.

Installed, not authored

The script body lives once, on the standards shelf: standards/filemaker/scripts/APP_CatalogRefresh.fmscript, with its reasoning in the app catalog scripts notes. This page is the pointer D-037 asks each app to hold instead of a copy. Nothing here is the script.

docs.title: Install values in this file
docs.text:
• Script name: refresh | Target_Tables, matching this file's <verb> | <object> convention rather than the shelf's APP_CatalogRefresh filename. The shelf names the definition; each file names its own script.
  • $layoutTables: view | Target_Tables, the layout on the view_Target_Tables occurrence. The only line edited at install. The shelf copy ships it empty and refuses to run until it is set, so no app's naming rides along inside a shared file.
  • Placement: 00_APP, on OnFirstWindowOpen and on a developer button.

docs.title: What it writes here
docs.text: One Target_Tables row per base table that has a field defined. It owns fm_BaseTableName, isPresent, LastSeenAt and AuditField_gaps. It never writes fm_BaseTableID, which is typed from the DDR export (D-050), and never writes a display field.

docs.title: First run, 2026-10-23
docs.text:
Clean on the first attempt. 22 base tables found, 22 rows created, 0 gone, 0 failing the audit, 22 waiting on a DDR id.

Two things that run proved beyond the script itself:

  • Every base table in this file conforms to the data standards. PrimaryKey and all four audit fields are present on all of them, which is the first time that has been checked rather than assumed, and it held across a schema built over three sittings.
  • No table is invisible. The count matched Manage Database exactly, so no base table is sitting there without a field defined, which is the one blind spot of reading FileMaker_BaseTableFields on FileMaker 19.

The catalog table lists itself, which is correct: it is a base table like any other.

docs.title: Why the names here became the standard's names
docs.text:
This is the first file in any solution to build the catalog, so its names are the ones the standard adopted: Target_Tables over D-043's proposed APP_TABLES (D-049), and AuditField_gaps over the proposed AuditGap. Nothing about either name is specific to people or to URITP; they describe a table catalog in any FileMaker file. A proposed name that was never built lost to a name that exists, which is the test D-049 applied.

The two things that genuinely are local are handled as local: the layout and script names, set at install, and FileMaker 19's inability to report a base-table id, which is a version condition rather than an app condition and is written into the standard as such.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Seed fm_BaseTableID for all 22 rows from the DDR export, then run again. New rows and waiting-on-an-id should both read 0, and that count stays at 0 until a table is added.

docs.title: SYNC_Run
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: SYNC_Run
docs.text:
The orchestrator. Reads one source's context, opens a session, calls pull then dispatch then push, and shows the session.

Grain

One press of Sync for one source. Everything else is a subscript.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Reads the source, its container and its system in a single ExecuteSQL join (D-048 ruling 6), packs the result into a context JSON, opens a sync_SESSIONS row, and calls three scripts in order: the pull adapter, the dispatcher and the push adapter. If the pull fails, it stops and shows the session (which still exists, with whatever error events the pull wrote). On success it navigates to the session record so the user sees the outcome.

docs.title: The context block
docs.text:
Every subscript receives the same JSON: session, source, container, viewPath, listID, containerName, system, systemName, baseURL, token. The context is read once, and nothing downstream looks it up again. A token never appears in a script parameter visible to the user because SYNC_Run is a button script invoked with a source name, and the subscripts receive machine keys that only become a token inside the adapter.

If the source's system is not ClickUp, the push is skipped. That is the only branch on systemName in this script. The pull adapter already dispatches by system (through the context block's systemName), and the dispatcher is system-agnostic.

docs.title: The one context join
docs.text:
Nine columns across three tables:

sync_SOURCES.PrimaryKey
sync_SOURCES.fk_xtContainer
sync_SOURCES.xt_ViewPath
xt_CONTAINERS.xt_ID
xt_CONTAINERS.Name
xt_SYSTEMS.PrimaryKey
xt_SYSTEMS.Name
xt_SYSTEMS.BaseURL
xt_SYSTEMS.Token

The alternative (relationships through sync_SOURCES_fxtContainers) would expose the same data through the graph and add two table occurrences. Both are equivalent for the subscripts, which receive variables either way. The SQL was chosen because the graph was just rebuilt and the join is read-only.

docs.title: Param and result
docs.text:
Param: a sync_SOURCES Name as plain text.

Result: { "ok" : 1|0, "session" : "<PrimaryKey>", "pulled" : n, "dispatched" : n, "pushed" : n }

docs.title: D-043 gap
docs.text:
Field names in the SQL are literal text, matching the same gap flagged in XT_Refresh_Fields. The sql/ custom-function family needed to use GetFieldName in SQL does not exist yet. A rename of any joined field name breaks this script silently.

docs.title: XT_Refresh_Fields
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: XT_Refresh_Fields
docs.text:
The generic field-refresh dispatcher. Resolves a container's system and performs that system's adapter. Knows no API.

Grain

One container per run. Refreshes the xt_FIELDS rows under it.

docs.title: Why it exists separately from the adapter
docs.text:
D-046 reserves knowledge of an outside system's shape for ADAPTER_<System>_ scripts. A refresh that parsed ClickUp's JSON under a generic XT_ name would break that on the first script written, and the generic layer is the entire reason a second system costs an adapter instead of a rewrite.

Michael ruled the dispatcher shape on 2026-10-23, over the simpler option of naming the whole thing an adapter. It costs one extra script now and buys the pattern every future refresh reuses. SYNC_Dispatch already has this shape, so it is the file's second use of it rather than a new idea.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Reads the container and the system that owns it in one ExecuteSQL join, matching D-048's ruling that this layer reads its context that way. Then it branches on the system's Name and performs that adapter, returning the adapter's own result untouched.

A system with no adapter yet is named in the dialog, along with the script that would need writing. The one thing it must never do is fail quietly: an empty refresh and a refresh that could not run look identical in the data.

docs.title: The token never travels
docs.text: The adapter receives two keys, the container and the system, and reads BaseURL and Token off the system record itself. A token passed as a script parameter is visible in the Data Viewer and in any error dialog that echoes the parameter, and STEPS.md already confirmed no token appears in script text. Passing keys keeps that true.

docs.title: Param and result
docs.text:
Param: { "container" : "<xt_CONTAINERS PrimaryKey>" }

Result: { "ok" : 1|0, "system" : "<name>", "updated" : n, "missing" : n, "native" : n }

docs.title: Two things flagged rather than hidden
docs.text:
The SQL is not built from GetFieldName, and D-043 says it should be

D-043 settled that SQL text is built from GetFieldName so a rename follows the field. GetFieldName returns TO::Field, which is not valid in a FileMaker SQL statement, so following that rule needs a helper custom function to strip the occurrence prefix. No such family exists on the standards shelf: json-params, color and json-mutate are the three. So this script and the adapter both name fields as literal text, which means a rename of fk_xtSystem or xt_ID breaks them silently. A sql/ custom-function family is the real fix and is a decision Michael has not been asked for yet.

The branch on $systemName is a string comparison against the system record's Name. That is the one place a renamed xt_SYSTEMS row would break dispatch. Keying the branch on the system's PrimaryKey instead would be rename-proof but unreadable in the script; left as a name deliberately.

A contact-sheet line is the owner's name, a label and a value. Venues, the program's inboxes and a show's stage management inbox all print on the same sheet as people because they all have cards. A distro list is a set of those lines, not a table.

docs.title: FileMaker is canonical
docs.text: A person can be born in ClickUp, typed in by name on a phone. The next sync adopts them: it creates the PEOPLE record and links it to the task with one row in XTERNAL_JOINS. From then on FileMaker wins. A difference ClickUp shows later lands in sync_RECONCILE for a decision and never overwrites a field by itself.

docs.title: No ClickUp id on this table
docs.text: The link to a task is a join row, never a field here. Nothing on PEOPLE knows ClickUp exists, which is what lets the same person be linked to another system later without touching this table.

docs.title: No email or phone on this table
docs.text: Contact values live on the person's CONTACTS card. The primary email is the first related email by sort_Index. There is no stored copy, because a stored copy goes stale the moment an address is added, corrected or reordered, and nothing says so.

docs.title: The playbill name is a fact
docs.text: stored_NameDisplayInPlaybills fills itself once from first and last name and is then edited by hand to whatever the playbill should print. It is not a copy of anything and must never be cleaned up as a derivable value.

docs.title: Empty optional names are true
docs.text:
Preferred name, alternate name and pronouns are empty for many people. That is a fact about the person, not a missing value.

docs.title: Refreshed, never typed, except the id
docs.text:
The refresh reads SELECT DISTINCT BaseTableName FROM FileMaker_BaseTableFields, finds each name, and writes presence, last-seen and the audit gap. A table that disappears keeps its row with isPresent at 0, because a container may still point at it.

fm_BaseTableID is the one typed field. It comes from the DDR export, because no FileMaker 19 function or system table reports a base-table id. Empty is meaningful: a row the refresh created that nobody has seeded yet. Find isPresent 1 with an empty id and that is the worklist; the refresh's closing dialog counts it for you.

docs.title: AuditField_gaps is the conformance report
docs.text:
Every base table is supposed to carry PrimaryKey and the four audit fields. Nothing in FileMaker enforces that, so the refresh compares each table's real field list against the five and writes what is missing, one per line. Empty means the table conforms, and a find on a non-empty AuditField_gaps is the whole audit. The closing dialog also names the tables that failed.

It matters here more than most files: every join in this schema keys on PrimaryKey, so a table missing one never matches rather than erroring, and the sync layer reads the audit fields for provenance when a reconcile row asks who changed what.

Rewritten on every run and never typed, so it cannot go stale and claim a table conforms when it stopped conforming.

docs.title: This is the app catalog
docs.text:
Ruled 2026-10-23, D-049: this table is the app catalog's table half under its built name, and APP_TABLES was never created in any file. APP_CatalogRefresh on the standards shelf writes here, and the app catalog carries the name. The superseded APP_TABLES page in this folder points back to this one.

The standard calls the conformance field AuditGap; this file built it as AuditField_gaps, and the built name wins for the same reason Target_Tables did. No other solution has the field.

Still open: the file has no layout catalog, so whether it becomes Target_Layouts or APP_LAYOUTS is unruled. And a renamed base table reads as one gone plus one new until the file moves to FileMaker 2023, where the id becomes readable and the rename becomes invisible.

- What elements of the artowrk inspired your implementation of the same theme?

- What similar contrasts did you choose to make between the artwork and your cue?

docs.title: The app catalog
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: The app catalog
docs.text: Every FileMaker file keeps a record of its own tables, generated from the file itself, carrying only what FileMaker cannot store. On FileMaker 19 the base-table id is typed from the DDR, because the file cannot report it.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Every solution carries a table catalog, Target_Tables, with one record per base table in the file. Anything else in the file that needs to point at a table points at a catalog record rather than naming the table in text.

A layout catalog is the same idea one object type over, and the app's navigation menu is that catalog. It is specified below as APP_LAYOUTS, but no file has built one yet, so that name is a proposal and not a fact.

The field registers live once, here, in tables/. An app's own table notes point at them rather than copying them.

docs.title: Generated, never typed, with one exception
docs.text:
FileMaker already knows its tables. A list someone maintains by hand is a second copy of the schema and it drifts the first time a table is renamed. So presence, the current name, and last-seen are written only by APP_CatalogRefresh, which reads the file's own schema tables. People type only the things FileMaker has no place for.

The exception is fm_BaseTableID, and it exists because of a platform limit rather than a choice. See the version section.

docs.title: The key, and why it is a name on FileMaker 19
docs.text:
A base-table id cannot be read on FileMaker 19

FileMaker_BaseTables, BaseTableNames and BaseTableIDs all arrived in FileMaker 2023 (20.1). FileMaker_BaseTableFields arrived in 19.4.1 and carries base-table names and their fields, but no table id. FileMaker_Tables.TableId is a table occurrence id, the wrong grain, several per base table. This standard previously claimed the base-table system table shipped in 19.4; that was never true and was never run (corrected 2026-10-23).

On FileMaker 2023 and later the id is the key, it is read from the file, and a rename is invisible to everything pointing at a catalog record. That is the design and it still is.

On FileMaker 19.4.1 the refresh matches on fm_BaseTableName, and fm_BaseTableID is typed once per table from the DDR export, which does carry real ids (D-050). Empty is meaningful: a row the refresh created and nobody has seeded. Find isPresent 1 with an empty id and that is the worklist, reported in the refresh's closing dialog.

The cost is named rather than hidden: a renamed base table reads as one gone and one new. Nothing in a 19 file can say otherwise. Move the id across by hand or reseed from the next DDR. The id key existed to make renames safe, and on 19 a rename can only be noticed, not absorbed.

docs.title: What gets typed
docs.text:
On the table catalog: fm_BaseTableID until the platform can report it, plus a display name, whether ClickUp feeds the table, and notes. On the layout catalog: a display name, a menu section, an order within the section, whether it shows in the menu, and notes. If a value can be read from the file, it is not typed.

Target_Tables as it stands in URITP People carries none of the display fields yet, only identity. They are added when something needs them, per D-035.

docs.title: Gone, never deleted
docs.text:
A table the refresh no longer finds keeps its row with isPresent at 0. The record stays, because other records may point at it, and a record that silently loses its target is worse than one that says the target is gone. Rebuild it in the file and the next refresh reverses the flag.

LastSeenAt answers when a table was last seen, which is why no removal timestamp is carried.

docs.title: Self-audit
docs.text:
The refresh checks every base table for the standard fields in the data standards: PrimaryKey and the four audit fields. This check works on 19.4.1, because FileMaker_BaseTableFields reports every field of every base table.

The conformance report does not exist yet

What is missing is meant to land in AuditGap, one field per line, so that an empty AuditGap means the table conforms and a find on that field is the conformance report. Target_Tables has no such field, so the refresh computes the gap and discards it. Adding AuditGap as Text, plus one Set Field in the refresh, is all this needs, and the computation is already proven.

docs.title: What else the refresh does on its own
docs.text:
More than the id limit suggests: it finds a table it has never seen, notices one that has vanished, keeps presence and last-seen true on every row, computes the conformance gap per table, and counts the file's base tables. The only manual act is typing an id for a table just added, and base tables are a finite set that changes rarely.

A base table with no fields defined does not appear in FileMaker_BaseTableFields and so is invisible to the refresh. It stops mattering the moment the table has a field.

docs.title: The menu
docs.text: APP_OpenMenu opens a card window on the APP_MENU layout, found to layouts marked for the menu and not removed, sorted by section then order. Each row's button runs APP_GoToLayout with the layout's id. That script looks up the layout's current name from its id at the moment of the click, so renaming a layout never breaks a menu entry. None of this runs until a file has a layout catalog.

docs.title: Installing it in an app
docs.text:
• Target_Tables, field for field as the register.
  • A layout on an occurrence of Target_Tables, a utility form. The refresh navigates to it, so it stops cold without one. Its name goes in $layoutTables at the top of the refresh; nothing else is edited.
  • Script folder 00_APP, typed or pasted from scripts/: APP_CatalogRefresh, and APP_GoToLayout and APP_OpenMenu once there is a layout catalog to drive them.
  • APP_CatalogRefresh on the file's OnFirstWindowOpen trigger, and on a developer button for after schema work.
  • Run it, then seed fm_BaseTableID for every row from the DDR export, then run it again and confirm nothing new appears.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
19.4.1 is the floor. That is when FileMaker_BaseTableFields arrived, and the refresh reads nothing else. Below it the refresh says so and stops.

FileMaker 2023 (20.1) is where this standard wants to live. FileMaker_BaseTables gives the base-table id directly, which makes the id the key again, makes renames safe, and makes fm_BaseTableID generated rather than typed. The layout half uses LayoutIDs and LayoutNames, which every supported version has.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
It is not the spec. The catalog records what exists in the file; the app package in this repo records what the file is built toward. Exporting the catalog and laying it beside the package's tables/ folder is a punch list, and like any punch list it is temporary.

It does not make SQL rename-safe. ExecuteSQL names table occurrences and fields, not base tables. That job belongs to GetFieldName, in the data standards.

docs.title: Why the name is Target_Tables
docs.text:
D-043 called this table APP_TABLES. URITP People built it as Target_Tables and Michael ruled on 2026-10-23 that the built name stands (D-049). The standard follows the file rather than the other way round, because no other solution had built the catalog at all, so there was nothing to keep compatible and no reason to carry the weaker name forward.

docs.title: Clipboard snippets
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: Clipboard snippets
docs.text: How a script written in this repo gets into FileMaker without retyping it. The fmp-renderer turns the .fmscript into FileMaker's clipboard format on demand; nothing generated is stored.

docs.title: Why plain text does not paste
docs.text: FileMaker's Script Workspace ignores ordinary text on the clipboard. It only accepts steps in its own XML, fmxmlsnippet, carried under a private clipboard type, XMSS. Copy a .fmscript from GitHub and paste it, and nothing happens. Proven on URITP People's PEOPLE_Compare, 89 steps, 2026-10-05.

docs.title: The .fmscript is the only source
docs.text: A script lives here once, as its readable .fmscript. Its XML is derived, so it is never committed: a stored copy is a second version of the script that drifts the first time someone edits one and not the other.

docs.title: Getting a script into FileMaker
docs.text:
Open the app in the fmp-renderer, go to Scripts, pick the script, press Copy for FileMaker. The renderer reads the .fmscript, builds the XML in the browser, and copies a one-line Terminal command with the XML baked in. Paste it into Terminal, press Enter, click into an empty script in FileMaker, press ⌘V. Nothing touches the disk, so it does not matter where or whether the repo is checked out.

A browser cannot put FileMaker's private clipboard type on the clipboard itself, which is the only reason Terminal is in the loop.

docs.title: Steps that do not translate yet
docs.text:
The renderer translates only steps whose XML has been proven by a real paste. Any other step pastes as a comment reading TYPE BY HAND: followed by the original line, and shows in red before you copy, so a script never pastes silently short. Type those few by hand.

To teach the renderer a new step: build it once in FileMaker, copy it, and read what FileMaker wrote. This command saves the clipboard's steps to a file:

osascript -e 'the clipboard as «class XMSS»' | sed 's/^«data XMSS//; s/»$//' | xxd -r -p > step.xml

That file is what the translation for the step gets written from, so the renderer only ever writes XML FileMaker itself produced.

docs.title: What resolves on paste
docs.text:
Fields resolve by table occurrence and field name, so a script written against the file's real names pastes cleanly. A name that does not exist pastes as a missing-field marker rather than failing, which makes it easy to find. Check every Go to Layout step after a paste.

docs.title: App catalog scripts
docs.text: MAW Prose · Fall 2026

docs.title: App catalog scripts
docs.text:
APP_CatalogRefresh, APP_GoToLayout and APP_OpenMenu. What each one does, what FileMaker 19 cannot tell it, and the checks on a first install.

Copy targets in this folder, installed into each app's 00_APP script folder. The standard they serve is the app catalog.

docs.title: APP_CatalogRefresh
docs.text:
Reads every base table that has a field defined, adds a Target_Tables row for one it has not seen, stamps isPresent and LastSeenAt on every row it does see, flips isPresent to 0 on a row it stops seeing, and reports what changed in a dialog. It never writes a typed field, and it never writes fm_BaseTableID.

The upsert finds by name once per table. A file has tens of tables, not thousands, so a find per row costs nothing and keeps the script plain.

docs.title: What FileMaker 19 cannot tell it
docs.text:
There is no base-table id available on 19. FileMaker_BaseTables, BaseTableNames and BaseTableIDs all arrived in FileMaker 2023 (20.1). FileMaker_Tables.TableId is a table occurrence id, the wrong grain, several per base table. FileMaker_BaseTableFields arrived in 19.4.1 and carries names and fields but no table id.

So the refresh matches on fm_BaseTableName, and fm_BaseTableID is typed by hand from the DDR export (D-050). Three consequences, all of them designed around rather than hidden:

  • Empty is the worklist. A row the script creates has no id, and the script's closing dialog counts the rows waiting for one. A find on isPresent 1 with fm_BaseTableID empty is the to-do list, and it is never a guess about which tables are new.
  • A rename looks like a deletion plus an addition. Nothing in the file can tell the refresh otherwise. Rename a base table and you get the old row flipped to isPresent 0 and a fresh row with no id; move the id across by hand, or reseed from the next DDR. This is the exact failure the id key existed to prevent, and on 19 it cannot be prevented, only noticed.
  • A table with no fields defined is invisible. FileMaker_BaseTableFields only lists tables that have at least one field. Not a bug, a 19 limit; it stops mattering the moment the table has a field.

Upgrading to FileMaker 2023 removes all three. Until then this is the honest version.

docs.title: What is still automatic
docs.text: More than the id situation suggests. The script detects a new table, detects a vanished one, maintains presence and last-seen on every row, computes the D-043 conformance gap per table from FileMaker_BaseTableFields, and counts the file's base tables for the dialog. The only manual act is typing an id for a table you just added, and tables are a finite, rarely changing set.

docs.title: The layout name is an install variable
docs.text: $layoutTables is set in the first steps and is the only line an installing app edits. The script needs record context, which means a layout whose base table occurrence is the catalog table; it does not care what that layout is called. URITP People's is view | Target_Tables, on the view_Target_Tables occurrence. A missing layout stops the script with a dialog naming the variable, rather than letting Go to Layout fail quietly and writing records into whatever context happened to be current.

docs.title: AuditGap has nowhere to land
docs.text: The script computes the missing standard fields into $gap, because that is the D-043 conformance check, but Target_Tables has no field to hold it, so nothing is written and a comment step says so. This one is worth closing: the gap computation genuinely works on 19.4.1, so adding AuditGap as Text and one Set Field turns a find on that field into the conformance report.

docs.title: The layout catalog
docs.text: No file has one, so there is no built name to follow and inventing one would be a guess. Whether it becomes Target_Layouts for symmetry or stays APP_LAYOUTS is unruled, and the layout half has been cut from this script until a file has the table. APP_GoToLayout and APP_OpenMenu below are unreachable meanwhile.

docs.title: APP_GoToLayout
docs.text: Looks up the layout's current name from its id at the moment it runs. When it runs from the APP_MENU card it closes the card first, so the move happens in the window underneath.

docs.title: APP_OpenMenu
docs.text: Opens APP_MENU as a card, found to ShowInMenu and not removed, in the layout's restored sort: MenuSection, then MenuOrder.

docs.title: Check on the first install
docs.text:
• That $layoutTables names a layout that exists in this file, on an occurrence of the catalog table. The script tells you if it does not.
  • That the base-table list comes back at all. A leading ? or an empty result means the file is older than 19.4.1.
  • That the dialog's base-table count matches the Tables tab of Manage Database. If it is short, a table has no fields defined.
  • That running it twice creates nothing the second time. That is the proof the name match works.
  • That Get ( WindowStyle ) reports 3 for a card window, once there is a menu to open.
